project.name: Mantine Dashboard Builder
project.summary: A dashboard builder that runs in the browser: an app frame around a canvas of charts, numbers and tables, fed by swappable data sources. A small helper server (the relay) runs the database queries a browser can't.

issues.title: A secret key is written into athenaRuntime.test.ts
issues.detail: Athena tests (src/plugins/optional/aws/athenaRuntime.test.ts) contains an Amazon Web Services (AWS) access key. Anyone who can see the code can use it to get into AWS as you. Treat it as leaked: move it out of the code and replace it with a new one.

notes.f:src/plugins/optional/aws/athenaRuntime: line 16: an Amazon Web Services (AWS) access key (starts “AKIA…”, 20 characters)

issues.fix:
Security fix: hard-coded secrets. Do not print, echo or repeat any secret value in your replies, commits or logs.

These lines contain a secret written directly in the code:
- src/plugins/optional/aws/athenaRuntime.test.ts:16: an Amazon Web Services (AWS) access key

For each one:
1. Replace the literal with an environment variable lookup (process.env.NAME in JavaScript/TypeScript), using a clear variable name. If the app can't run without it, fail with a clear error when it is missing instead of falling back to a hard-coded value.
2. Add each variable name (with an empty value, never the real one) to .env.example, and make sure .env is listed in .gitignore.
3. Update any deployment config (Docker, Cloud Run, Vercel, etc.) so the variable is set in production.
4. Run the app or its tests to confirm it still starts with the variables set.

Then give me a short checklist (without the values) of which services these keys belong to, so I can rotate each one: create a new key in that service's dashboard, put it in my environment, and revoke the old one. Because the old values are in git history, assume they are compromised.
